question: How much of the observed nearest-two prediction failure is explained by using only two donors, versus the information gained by selecting those two donors using phylogenetic proximity?
fixed_units: Same 47 held-out tips, 21 fixed log1p TPM10K genes, six exact six-bit pigment-presence classes, no source/feature/threshold changes
same_fold_error: training-only among-other-46-species gene variance as already frozen
derivation: For the m=n_state-1 eligible other-species donors of one held-out tip and gene, the expected squared error of uniformly sampling a pair of donors WITHOUT REPLACEMENT equals (target - full-donor-class mean)^2 + [(m-2)/(2*(m-1))]*popvariance among the m donor measurements. This is an exact finite-population identity, conditional on the observed data; not an evolutionary process model.
rule: For each heldout tip, average all 21 fixed genes after dividing by frozen fold-specific training variance; then mean equally over 47 tips. Only the random-two expected prediction error is new.
interpretation: If both small_donor_penalty and locality_gain_over_random2 are positive and penalty exceeds gain, small-k donor-mean variance can explain the signed net failure despite a useful phylogenetic locality effect.
inference: Descriptive exact algebra only. No new P value, no new k choice, no alternative gene selection, no claims of independent replication or biological causation.
